title: How To Never Again Take Misbehavior Personally https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2021/12/10/how-to-never-again-take-misbehavior-personally/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that teachers who take student misbehavior personally undermine their own management by absorbing emotional weight that should stay with the student. He explains that visible frustration, anger, or hurt signals to students that their actions are affecting the teacher, which shifts responsibility away from the student and hands them power to keep pushing the same buttons. He draws on Alfred Adler's concept of 'separation of tasks' — the principle that healthy relationships depend on each person owning only their own responsibilities — to argue that a teacher's task is to run their classroom management plan well, not to manage how students feel about their own consequences. He redefines compassion in this context: not permissiveness, but protecting every student's right to learn without interference, while calmly letting students feel the natural weight of their choices. The piece frames emotional detachment from misbehavior, paired with an unwavering plan, as both healthier for the teacher and more effective for changing student behavior.
points: Visible emotional reactions to misbehavior — frustration, anger, hurt — signal to students that their actions affect the teacher and shift responsibility away from them.
Alfred Adler's 'separation of tasks' concept is applied to argue that a teacher's job is to run their management plan, not to carry students' emotional burdens.
Simply becoming aware of one's emotional reaction to misbehavior can, by itself, be enough to remain calm regardless of the behavior displayed.
Compassion in a classroom means protecting every student's right to learn without interference, not permissiveness or absorbing their consequences emotionally.
Letting a classroom management plan do its job, without yelling, scolding, or lecturing, benefits both the teacher's wellbeing and the student's long-term development.
quotes: If you take misbehavior personally, then you’re weakening your ability to manage your classroom.
When you feel frustration, anger, or hurt in response to misbehavior, you’re taking its burden upon yourself.
Just knowing is half the battle and can be all the impetus you need to remain calm no matter the behavior. Just water off a duck’s back.
Adler believed, and millions can attest, that healthy relationships stem from what he called a “separation of tasks.” A separation of tasks entails focusing solely on what are your responsibilities.
Compassion in a school setting is protecting every student’s right to learn and enjoy school and your right to teach them without interference.

It’s embracing your responsibility, which is to teach great lessons and provide a clean and safe environment, and then shifting in total the responsibility to listen, learn, and behave where it belongs.
